chapter.name: Arithmetic Progressions
chapter.blurb: Reena's rising salary, a ladder's shortening rungs and Shakila's growing money box motivate the arithmetic progression: a list where a fixed number, the common difference, is added to each term to get the next. The chapter builds the formula for the nth term, learns to run it backwards to find a term's position or test whether a number belongs to a list, solves for an unknown term or common difference from two given terms, and (following Gauss's schoolboy trick of pairing a list with its reverse) derives and applies the formula for the sum of the first n terms, including the case where solving for the number of terms gives a quadratic with two valid answers.

scope_in.item: Recognise an arithmetic progression (AP) as a list where each term after the first is obtained by adding one fixed number, the common difference d, to the term before it; know that d may be positive, negative or zero
Write the general form of an AP, a, a+d, a+2d, a+3d, ..., and list an AP given its first term a and common difference d
Distinguish a finite AP (has a last term) from an infinite AP (has no last term)
Test whether a given list of numbers is an AP by checking that a_(k+1) - a_k is the same for every consecutive pair, and find a and d for a list that is an AP
Given three consecutive terms a, b, c of an AP, use b = (a + c)/2 (the arithmetic mean of a and c)
Find the nth term (general term) of an AP using a_n = a + (n - 1)d, including the last term l of a finite AP
Use the nth term formula in reverse: find n given a_n, decide whether a given number is a term of an AP (n must come out a positive integer), and find which term (if any) equals zero
Determine an AP (find a and d) from two given terms by forming and solving a pair of linear equations
Find the nth term of a finite AP counted from the last term, either by locating the total number of terms first or by reversing the AP (new first term l, new common difference -d)

Apply the nth term formula to word problems: counting terms of a described list, yearly simple interest as an AP (using Simple Interest = (P x R x T)/100), and similar real-life step-by-step growth or decline situations
Find the sum S_n of the first n terms of an AP using S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d], and using S_n = (n/2)(a + l) when the last term is known instead of d
Use the relation a_n = S_n - S_(n-1) to get a term from two sums
Find the sum of the first n positive integers, S_n = n(n + 1)/2, as a special case
Given the nth term of a list as an explicit linear formula in n (e.g. a_n = 3 + 2n), decide it is an AP and read off a and d
Solve the sum formula for a missing quantity (a, d, or n) when the other three of S, a, d, n are known, including the quadratic-in-n case, recognising that two positive values of n can both be valid
Solve multi-part AP word problems combining the nth term and the sum of n terms (e.g. production or savings problems)

scope_out.item: Geometric progressions (multiplying by a fixed number each time, e.g. the 5/4-every-3-years savings scheme on p. 49) and any GP formulas

scope_out.reason: Squares (1^2, 2^2, 3^2, p. 50) and the Fibonacci-type rabbit sequence (p. 50) are given only as examples of patterns that are NOT arithmetic progressions; no formula for summing them is developed in this chapter.

scope_out.item: Inserting a given number of arithmetic means between two numbers, or general arithmetic-mean theory beyond three consecutive terms
scope_out.reason: The chapter's only arithmetic-mean statement is the single closing note b = (a+c)/2 for three consecutive terms a, b, c (p. 72); a fuller treatment is not given here.

concepts.name: Meaning of an AP: term, common difference, general form
concepts.description: A sequence in which each term after the first is obtained by adding one fixed number, the common difference d, to the term before it; the general form a, a+d, a+2d, ...; finite APs (with a last term) versus infinite APs (without one).
concepts.idea: An AP is a list built by repeatedly adding the same fixed number to get from one term to the next.
concepts.rule: If a_1, a_2, a_3, ... is an AP with first term a and common difference d, then a_2 - a_1 = a_3 - a_2 = ... = d, and the general form is a, a+d, a+2d, a+3d, .... d can be positive, negative or zero. A finite AP has a last term; an infinite AP does not.
concepts.example: Reena's salary 8000, 8500, 9000, ... (p. 49) is an AP with a = 8000, d = 500. The ladder rungs 45, 43, 41, ..., 31 (p. 49) form an AP with a = 45, d = -2. With a = 2, d = 0 the AP is 2, 2, 2, 2, ... (p. 53).

concepts.name: Testing whether a list is an AP; finding a and d
concepts.description: Deciding whether a given list of numbers is an AP by checking that consecutive differences are equal, finding a and d when it is one, recognising non-AP patterns, and the three-consecutive-term arithmetic-mean fact b = (a+c)/2.
concepts.idea: A list is an AP exactly when the difference between every pair of consecutive terms is the same fixed value.
concepts.rule: Compute a_2 - a_1, a_3 - a_2, a_4 - a_3, .... If all are equal, the list is an AP with that value as d; if even one pair differs, it is not. Always subtract the earlier term from the later one, a_(k+1) - a_k, even when the later term is smaller. If a, b, c are three consecutive terms of an AP, b = (a + c)/2.
concepts.example: For 4, 10, 16, 22, ...: a_2 - a_1 = 6, a_3 - a_2 = 6, a_4 - a_3 = 6, so it is an AP, d = 6 (p. 54). For 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, ...: the differences 0, 1, 1, 2 are not equal, so it is not an AP (p. 53).

concepts.idea: The same formula a_n = a + (n - 1)d can be solved for n when the term's value is known, which tells us which position a given number occupies -- or shows it never occurs.
concepts.rule: Set a + (n - 1)d equal to the given value and solve for n; n must be a positive integer for the value to actually be a term of the AP. Setting a_n = 0 and solving for n (if it gives a positive integer) finds which term, if any, is zero.
concepts.example: AP 21, 18, 15, ...: solving -81 = 21 + (n - 1)(-3) gives n = 35, so -81 is the 35th term (Example 4, p. 58); the same AP has its 8th term equal to 0. AP 5, 11, 17, 23, ...: solving 301 = 5 + (n - 1) x 6 gives n = 302/6, not a whole number, so 301 is never a term (Example 6, p. 59).

concepts.name: Finding an AP from two given terms; the nth term from the end
concepts.description: Setting up and solving two simultaneous linear equations in a and d from two given terms of an AP, and finding the nth term of a finite AP counted from its last term by either counting total terms or reversing the AP.
concepts.idea: Knowing any two terms of an AP is enough to pin down both a and d, because each given term supplies one linear equation in a and d; counting from the far end of a finite AP is the same as counting from the near end of its mirror image.
concepts.rule: a_m = a + (m - 1)d and a_k = a + (k - 1)d give two simultaneous linear equations in a and d; solve them together. For the pth term from the end of a finite AP of N terms, either find N first and use the (N - p + 1)th term from the start, or reverse the AP (new first term = old last term l, new common difference = -d) and find its pth term.
concepts.example: 3rd term = 5, 7th term = 9 gives a + 2d = 5 and a + 6d = 9, solving to a = 3, d = 1 (Example 5, p. 58). AP 10, 7, 4, ..., -62 has 25 terms; its 11th term from the end is the 15th term from the start, a_15 = 10 + 14 x (-3) = -32 (Example 8, pp. 59-60).

concepts.name: Word problems using the nth term formula
concepts.description: Translating an everyday situation that changes by a fixed amount at every step into an AP (identifying a and d), and applying a_n = a + (n - 1)d to answer 'how many' or 'what value at step n' questions, including simple interest.
concepts.idea: Many everyday situations that increase or decrease by a fixed amount each step are APs in disguise, and the nth term formula answers 'how many' or 'what value at step n' questions about them.
concepts.rule: Translate the situation into a, d (and sometimes a_n or n), then apply a_n = a + (n - 1)d. Simple interest on a fixed sum forms an AP because SI = (P x R x T)/100 increases by the fixed amount (P x R)/100 for every extra year.
concepts.example: Two-digit numbers divisible by 3 form the AP 12, 15, ..., 99 with a = 12, d = 3; solving 99 = 12 + (n - 1) x 3 gives n = 30 (Example 7, p. 59). Simple interest of Rs 1000 at 8% p.a. gives yearly interest 80, 160, 240, ... an AP with a = 80, d = 80; the 30th year's interest is a_30 = 80 + 29 x 80 = Rs 2400 (Example 9, pp. 60-61). concepts.name: Sum of the first n terms of an AP
concepts.description: The two formulas S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d] and S_n = (n/2)(a + l) for the sum of the first n terms of an AP, the Gauss pairing idea behind the derivation, the relation a_n = S_n - S_(n-1), and the sum of the first n positive integers as a special case.
concepts.idea: Pairing the list with itself reversed turns the sum into n copies of the same pair-total, which is how both handy formulas for S_n are built.
concepts.rule: S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d] = (n/2)(a + a_n); when the last term l of a finite AP is known, S_n = (n/2)(a + l). Also a_n = S_n - S_(n-1).
concepts.example: Gauss's 1 + 2 + ... + 100 = 5050 by pairing (pp. 63-64). Shakila's money-box AP a = 100, d = 50, n = 21: S_21 = (21/2)[200 + 20 x 50] = 12600 (p. 65). Sum of first 1000 positive integers = (1000/2)(1 + 1000) = 500500 (Example 14(i), p. 66).

concepts.name: Solving the sum formula for an unknown; combined nth-term and sum problems
concepts.description: Solving S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d] for a missing quantity among S, a, d, n, including the quadratic-in-n case with two admissible roots; reading a and d off an explicit linear nth-term formula; multi-part word problems combining the nth term and the sum.
concepts.idea: The sum formula has four linked quantities (S, a, d, n) -- given any three, it can be solved for the fourth, sometimes via a quadratic in n with two valid answers.
concepts.rule: Substitute the three known quantities into S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d] (or use an explicit formula for a_n in terms of n to read off a and d) and solve for the missing one; a quadratic in n can have two positive-integer roots, both admissible, when some of the terms being summed are negative and cancel earlier positive ones.
concepts.example: AP 24, 21, 18, ...: solving 78 = (n/2)[48 + (n-1)(-3)] gives n = 4 or n = 13, both valid because terms 5 to 13 sum to zero (Example 13, pp. 65-66). Given a_n = 3 + 2n, a = 5 (value at n = 1) and d = 2 (coefficient of n). TV production a_3 = 600, a_7 = 700 gives d = 25, a = 550, a_10 = 775, S_7 = 4375 (Example 16, pp. 67-68).
